drills.title: vs Vijay-malu (823) — Three Knights Opening
drills.coachNote: The real danger wasn't the knight itself but where it could jump to — g6 forks your queen on e7 and your rook on f8 at once, and nothing you'd played yet stopped that. You played f6, kicking the knight, but that's exactly the square it wanted anyway: Ng6! Qf7 Nxf8 Rxf8, and White nets a full rook for a knight, swinging the game from roughly equal to nearly lost. Rfe8 sidesteps the whole problem by getting your rook off f8 before the fork ever exists, so lines like Nf3 Qd7 Qd2 Rxe1+ Rxe1 just trade down evenly. When a knight has a juicy fork square nearby, check whether your own move walks a piece onto it.

drills.title: vs Vijay-malu (823) — Three Knights Opening
drills.coachNote: White's d5 pawn was simply demanding your knight leave c6 — that part wasn't optional. You chose Nd4, which looks active and central, but d4 is covered by White's knight on f3: after Nxd4 exd4, White's queen jumps to g4 with real pressure, and you were forced into the purely defensive Qf6 just to hold things together, handing White a clean edge from what had been an even middlegame. Ne7 or Nb8 both answer the same pawn attack without landing on a covered square — quiet, safe retreats that keep your structure intact. Before relocating an attacked piece to a 'nice' square, always check who else is watching that square.
drills.threat: White's pawn on d5 is attacking your knight on c6, and it has to move somewhere safe this turn.

drills.title: vs belyjudegwapo (730) — Kings Pawn Opening
drills.coachNote: White's whole plan here was to shove the pawn through to d4, challenging your center and giving his cramped pieces room to breathe — that's the one thing that could make your huge advantage shrink. Bd7 did nothing to stop it, so White got d4 anyway, and after exd4 Nxd4 his knight sprang to a great central square and your +4.2 advantage dropped sharply toward a merely good position. d5 instead grabs the initiative first, hitting the bishop on e4 and locking the center on your terms — even desperate tries like Bxh7+ Kxh7 Nxe5 Bxe5 Bxe5 leave you firmly on top. When you're winning big, don't let the opponent get his central break for free — play it yourself.
drills.threat: White is looking to break with d4 and free his pieces, right while you're sitting on a completely winning position.

drills.coachNote: Your bishop has been sitting on a1 the whole time, deep in White's camp with nowhere to go — that's the piece White's rook on f1 is quietly circling. Kxf8 recaptured the bishop on f8 but completely ignored the one on a1, and the line Rxa1 Bf5 Nc5 f3 shows White simply picking it up for free, costing you a full piece even though you were already crushing at +7. Bd4+ is that same a1 bishop escaping with check — Kh1 is forced, and only then do you play Kxf8, followed by Nxf4 grabbing another pawn. Before recapturing, always take one extra look for your own hanging pieces, especially ones stranded in enemy territory.

drills.coachNote: Your bishop on g5 was doing real work — pinning the knight on f6 against the queen on d8 — but it was also under attack from Black's bishop on h6, and that needed an answer. Re1 ignored it, so Black just traded it off with Bxg5 Nxg5, and after Rg8 f4 you'd spent a tempo patching things up and the pin was gone, costing you a chunk of your edge. Bh4 keeps the exact same pin alive from one square back, out of the bishop's reach, so you stay comfortable and keep developing with Nbd2 and ideas like Bg3. When a piece of yours doing important work gets attacked, look for a retreat that keeps its job intact before reaching for a developing move elsewhere.

drills.coachNote: White's king never got to safety — it's sitting on e1 — and that's exactly the kind of target you want to keep attacking while you're already up nine pawns of advantage. Qe5 is a fine move but it sidesteps the check entirely, so after a3 Nc6 f4 Qe4 you were still winning easily, just with less bite than you had. Bb4+ uses that same diagonal to force Nc3, and then Bxc3+ bxc3 Qxc3+ Kf2 rips open White's queenside pawns with check after check, squeezing out even more material before the king finds any shelter. When you're already crushing, look first for the check that adds damage rather than the quiet move that just consolidates.

drills.coachNote: The real prize here was a pawn fork hitting the knight on c6 and the bishop on e6 together, but the knight on c6 needed dealing with first. Ng6 looks like its own fork, hitting the rook on f8 and the bishop on e7, but Black has the in-between Rf6!, attacking your knight directly; it has to flee with Nxf5, Black recaptures with Bxf5, and the whole advantage you had evaporates — which is exactly why this game ended in a draw instead of a win. Nxc6 first removes that defender, and after Qxc6 your pawn push d5 forks the queen and the bishop on e6, winning material cleanly once Black plays Qe8 dxe6 Rd8. Before committing to a flashy-looking fork, check whether the opponent has a forcing in-between move that lets the real piece escape.

drills.coachNote: Black's knight on f4 and bishop on e5 both eye your loose c3 pawn, but your bishop has its own target on Black's a6 — this is really a foot-race for whoever grabs the other's weak pawn first. Walking your king to e4 loses that race: Black plays Ne2, you shuffle with Kd5, and Bxc3 falls for free while you're nowhere near a6 — a balanced position becomes a clean pawn down. Be4 joins the race instead: after Ke6, Bb7, Nd5, your bishop lands Bxa6, so Black's eventual Bxc3 is just an even trade, not a loss. Keep pieces racing toward the weak pawn, not your king wandering.
